intro: Jerusalem artichokes are not true artichokes at all, but vigorous sunflower relatives grown for their knobbly underground tubers. They are hardy, reliable and useful for winter soups, stews and grated salads, with a sweet, nutty flavour which is not to everybody's taste and may not suit every digestion. The plants grow very tall in rich soil, making them useful as a screen or windbreak but also capable of robbing light from lower crops if planted in a long row. They are easy to grow from tubers, but hard to eradicate once established because even small pieces left in the soil can regrow.

Globe artichoke is a large, handsome thistle-family perennial grown for its unopened flower buds, unlike the underground tubers harvested from Jerusalem or Chinese artichokes. It is decorative enough for a border, with grey-green fern-like leaves and strong stems, but it needs more space than most vegetables and is not a natural choice for a very small garden. The reward is a distinctive, nutty crop: pick the heads while they are still tight and tender, before the scales open and the centre becomes tough. The plants establish quickly in rich, moist but well-drained soil, though they need regular watering, feeding, mulching and some protection in cold winters.

Asparagus is one of the finest spring vegetables: a long-lived perennial which gives a fresh, delicate crop just when the garden is short of new green shoots. It is not difficult once established, but it asks for space, clean ground and patience. Treat the bed as a permanent feature: clear perennial weeds thoroughly, improve the soil before planting and do not crop hard while the crowns are young. In return, a good bed can produce spears for many years, followed by tall ferny summer growth which feeds the roots for the next season.

Aubergines are decorative, heat-loving relatives of the tomato, grown for their glossy fruits as well as their purple flowers and large velvety leaves. They can crop well under glass or in a warm polytunnel, but outdoors they are a gamble except in very warm, sheltered places. The key requirement is heat: cool, grey weather slows growth and often delays fruiting until late summer. Treat aubergines as tender annuals, give them rich soil, steady moisture without waterlogging, and harvest the fruits while the skin still has its shine. Fruits may be oval, round or long, and varieties range from the familiar dark purple to white, violet and striped forms.

Broad beans are among the most dependable and useful garden crops. They are hardier than peas, will tolerate heavier soils than many beans, and can give fresh pods at a time when there is still relatively little else to pick. Autumn-sown plants often come through the winter and race away in early spring, while spring sowings provide the main summer crop. Each seed may produce several square-stemmed shoots, followed by scented black-and-white flowers and large pods containing green, white or sometimes reddish beans. Pick them young for the sweetest flavour; if left longer they become starchier but can be dried and stored as a useful winter food.

French beans are tender summer beans, grown for crisp young pods, fresh shelled flageolets or fully ripened dried haricots. They are far less hardy than broad beans and should not be rushed into cold soil, but once the weather is warm they are quick, colourful and productive. Dwarf types crop earliest and need no formal supports, although their low pods can be dirtied by rain or damaged by slugs. Climbing types take more work to set up, but they keep the pods off the soil, reduce bending at picking time and can crop for longer.

Runner beans are the classic British summer bean: vigorous, ornamental climbers with red, white, pink or bicoloured flowers and long flat pods that can crop heavily from late summer into autumn. They are less drought-tolerant than French beans and need a rich, moisture-retentive root run, so they flourish in moist, mild summers and struggle in hot, dry spells unless watered well. A row of runner beans also makes a useful screen or a colourful wigwam in a border, but the crop is not automatic: prepare the ground generously, provide strong supports, keep the roots moist after flowering and pick young pods every few days.

Leaf beets are a useful answer for gardeners who like spinach but find true spinach quick to bolt or difficult in dry weather. Swiss chard, seakale beet, spinach beet and perpetual spinach are all grown for leaves rather than swollen roots, and a few plants can provide many pickings over a long season. Swiss chard has broad leaves with thick, edible midribs, often white but sometimes red, yellow or pink, and it is ornamental enough for the flower border. Spinach beet has a plainer green leaf, is used much like spinach in the kitchen. The main rule is to pick regularly: small leaves are tender and useful for salads or cooking, while over-large leaves become tougher and the plant slows down.

Beetroot is much more than a boiled-and-pickled salad extra. Grown well, it has a sweet, earthy flavour, can be eaten raw in grated winter salads, cooked as a hot vegetable, used for borsch and chutneys, and even harvested for its young leaves. It is a cool-climate root crop that likes well-drained, humus-rich soil, steady moisture and no check to growth. It starts slowly, but once seedlings are established the roots swell quickly, especially if they are grown in short, repeated sowings or in module-raised clumps. Beetroot transplants better than many root crops, so early sowings under cover can give golf-ball-sized roots by late spring, while later sowings provide summer, autumn and storage roots.

Broccoli covers several related crops rather than just the green heads sold in supermarkets. Summer and autumn crops are mostly calabrese, which forms a central green head followed by side shoots, while winter and spring crops are usually purple or white sprouting broccoli, grown for a long succession of small spears when other fresh greens are scarce. Garden broccoli may not look as blemish-free as shop-bought heads, and summer crops often need protection from caterpillars and pigeons, but the flavour and the long season make it well worth growing.

Brussels sprouts are small cabbage-like buds produced up a tall stem, maturing gradually through autumn and winter. A freshly picked sprout from the garden is a midwinter treat, often sweeter and nuttier than shop-bought sprouts, and small firm buttons can be good raw as well as cooked. Success depends less on complicated technique than on firm, fertile soil, careful transplanting and steady growth. Cultivar choice, poor soil or badly checked growth can give open, leafy sprouts, while regular picking and removal of yellow leaves keep the crop clean and usable from October into March.

Cabbage is one of the most versatile brassicas, and with the right choice of variety it can provide food for much of the year. Spring cabbages give tender greens and small heads before many other vegetables are ready; summer and autumn cabbages provide fresh heads for salads, slaws and cooking; winter, savoy and red cabbages can stand or store into the colder months. The key is to match the variety to the season, because cabbage types differ in shape, texture, colour, hardiness and speed of hearting.

Capsicums include both sweet peppers and chillies: colourful, heat-loving members of the tomato and potato family. In their native climate they are perennial plants, but in Britain they are grown as tender annuals and are most reliable under glass or in a warm, sheltered position. Green peppers are edible but are still an immature stage; if left to ripen they change colour and, in many varieties, become sweeter or hotter and more deeply flavoured. That extra flavour comes at a cost, because ripe-coloured fruit take longer to develop and the plant produces fewer new peppers while they mature. The crop is therefore a balance between earlier, heavier green harvests and later, smaller harvests of fully coloured fruit.

Freshly pulled carrots have a sweet, earthy flavour that shop-bought roots rarely match. They are also one of the more awkward crops to establish well: germination can be slow, seedlings are vulnerable to slugs, and the roots need deep, fine, stone-free soil if they are to grow straight and tender. Once growing, however, carrots are very rewarding, especially if sown in short successions so that roots can be lifted from early summer into autumn. Good moisture, careful thinning, and protection from carrot fly make a big difference.

Cauliflower is one of the most rewarding brassicas, but also one of the least forgiving. The curd is a tight mass of flower buds, and the plant has to make strong, uninterrupted growth before it will produce a worthwhile head. Poor soil, loose planting, drought, overcrowding or a check after transplanting can all lead to tiny button heads or blind plants. Choose summer, autumn, overwintering or mini varieties to suit the season, and give them rich, firm soil, plenty of moisture and enough space.

Celeriac, or turnip-rooted celery, is grown for its swollen stem-base rather than for crisp stalks. It brings a strong earthy celery flavour to soups, stews, salads and winter dishes, and stores well into spring if lifted and kept cool. Although it avoids much of the blanching and earthing-up work of celery, it is still a long-season crop that needs rich, moisture-retentive soil, steady watering in dry weather and a good start under cover. The roots are fibrous and shallow, so growth is checked badly on dry ground; heavy, well-composted soil suits it especially well. Most varieties are quite similar, but all need the whole season to make a good-sized root.

Celery is a moisture-loving crop grown for crisp, strongly flavoured stems, and it is much easier to enjoy than to grow beautifully. Traditional trench celery is grown for winter flavour, but it demands deep preparation, regular watering and careful earthing-up to exclude light from the stems. Self-blanching celery is simpler because close planting and a dense canopy do much of the blanching work, although it is less hardy and usually best harvested before cold weather. Celery leaf is a useful lighter option, giving repeated pickings of smaller stems.

Chicory is grown in two useful ways: for green salad leaves in summer and autumn, and for pale, crisp chicons forced indoors to give fresh winter salad. The flavour is refreshing, tart and sometimes bitter, so it divides opinion, and excluding light produces paler, milder chicons. Forcing types such as Witloof are raised for their long roots, lifted in late autumn and brought into growth in dark, cool conditions; non-forcing types make larger lettuce-like heads for autumn use. The crop is generally healthy and not difficult, although forcing takes extra work and the roots are easiest to handle when grown in deep, loose soil.

Greenhouse cucumbers are the earliest and highest-yielding cucumbers, capable of producing fruit over a long season and sometimes almost daily in hot weather. They are also one of the more exacting greenhouse crops: seedlings need steady warmth, roots dislike cold wet compost, stems are brittle, and mature plants need careful watering, humid air, feeding, training and stopping. All-female varieties reduce flower-removal work, but check for occasional male flowers and follow the supplier’s instructions. Plants are usually trained vertically on strings, canes or wires, saving space and keeping the fruit clean.

Outdoor cucumbers are fast-growing, frost-tender cucurbits for the warmest part of the season. Modern ridge and outdoor F1 varieties can be smooth-skinned and mild-flavoured, while gherkins and apple cucumbers remain useful special cases.

Endive is a cool-season salad plant with more flavour and bitterness than lettuce, though less of lettuce's crispness. It can be eaten raw in mixed salads or cooked, and both curly-leaved frisée types and broader-leaved Batavian or escarole types are useful. Curly endive is usually for late-summer and autumn cutting, while broad-leaved endive is easier to grow for good hearts and is more useful in autumn and winter. The crop needs moisture, humus and some protection from heat or harsh frost; blanching, or choosing self-blanching varieties, gives paler, milder hearts. Small late-summer sowings can provide leaves and hearts into winter, with suitable protection in cold weather.

Florence fennel, or bulb fennel, is a sweet, aniseed-flavoured umbellifer grown for the swollen bases of its leaf-stalks. It belongs to the same broad family as carrot, parsnip and celeriac, but is eaten quite differently: sliced raw in salads, cooked gently for a soft creamy flavour, or used in soups and ratatouille. The feathery leaves are also edible, with a gentle aniseed flavour. Modern varieties have made it easier to grow by reducing the tendency to bolt before useful bulbs form. Match the variety to its sowing season and keep young plants growing steadily: drought, crowding or root checks can give stemmy plants instead of juicy bulbs. Summer sowings after an early crop are useful for autumn harvesting. Harvest while the bulbs are tender, before they become fibrous, stemmy or frosted.

Garlic is a hardy allium grown from individual cloves, usually planted in autumn for a summer harvest. Flavour varies with the variety, from mild cloves to strongly pungent types. Young plants tolerate very cold winter weather, fit conveniently into the garden after summer crops, and are lifted early enough to be followed by French beans, late brassicas or autumn salads.

Kale, also known as borecole, is a hardy, non-hearting brassica grown for its leaves and young spring shoots. It used to be treated as a plain winter standby, but modern varieties give a wide range of colours, textures and flavours, from deeply curled green leaves to red and flat-leaved types. It is one of the most dependable crops for autumn, winter and early spring, often standing when little else is available, and the flavour is generally better after frost.

Kohl rabi looks like a root crop, but the edible globe is really a swelling of the stem just above ground level. It is a cabbage relative with a sweet, mild brassica flavour and a delicate texture when grown quickly and picked young. The crop matures fast, often in about 8-12 weeks, making it useful as a half-season brassica. Quality depends on steady moisture and timely harvesting: drought, checks to growth or leaving the globes too long can make them hard and woody. Small young globes are good raw or cooked, while larger late varieties can stand into autumn if they keep growing steadily.

Leeks are among the most dependable alliums for a home garden, carrying the harvest from late summer through winter and, with the right varieties, into spring. They quietly gain size while summer crops fade, then provide sweet white shanks and useful green leaves when few fresh vegetables are available. Although closely related to onions, they are generally easier and more tolerant, especially in cool, moist conditions, but they still need a long season, steady moisture and some attention to blanching; most gardeners raise seedlings for transplanting.

Lettuce is one of the most useful crops for a British garden because it grows quickly from spring to autumn, thrives in cool, moist conditions and can be used either as cut-and-come-again leaves or as hearts. It is also one of the crops most often spoilt by casual treatment: slugs love young plants, hot dry weather encourages bolting and tipburn, and a whole sowing can mature at once if too many plants are grown for hearts.

Courgettes and marrows are the same general crop at different stages of use: courgettes are picked young, firm and tender, while marrows are allowed to grow larger and can be eaten fresh or stored. Modern courgette varieties are bred to keep producing small fruits, and a well-grown plant in summer warmth can be almost overwhelming, often giving several courgettes each week.

Squashes and pumpkins are vigorous cucurbits grown for fruits that range from tender summer squashes to hard-skinned winter keepers. Pick summer squashes young, mild and moist; winter squashes ripen with firm, sweet flesh and hard skins for winter or spring storage.

intro: The first flush of mushrooms is an exciting reward for careful indoor growing. This page covers cultivated button and chestnut mushrooms (Agaricus bisporus), grown in prepared mushroom compost. They need shelter from direct sunlight and can crop while outdoor vegetable beds are quiet. Fresh ready-spawned kits give the simplest start for small quantities; preparing mushroom compost from raw ingredients requires controlled composting and conditioning. Follow the supplier’s instructions for each stage. Other edible mushroom species need different substrates and growing conditions. For the simplest route, buy a fresh ready-spawned button-mushroom kit in a bag, bucket or box. Check the supplier’s start-by date and begin promptly; pre-started kits may already have completed much of the colonisation stage. Button mushrooms use a moist casing layer after the compost is colonised. Use the kit’s supplied or recommended casing and timing; not every mushroom species needs casing. Keep it moist without saturation. Pick button mushrooms at the size you prefer, before the veil opens for closed buttons or later for open caps.

Onions and shallots are among the most useful crops in the kitchen garden, providing fresh bulbs, salads, pickles and winter stores. Spring-planted sets offer a simple start; seed gives a wider choice of colours, sizes and seasonal types. Shallot bulbs usually divide into clusters, while overwintered onions provide earlier harvests.

Onions and shallots are among the most useful crops in the kitchen garden, providing fresh bulbs, salads, pickles and winter stores. Spring-planted sets offer a simple start; seed gives a wider choice of colours, sizes and seasonal types. Shallot bulbs usually divide into clusters, while overwintered onions provide earlier harvests.

Oriental leaves are a loose group of quick-growing salad and stir-fry crops, most of them brassicas, which are especially useful after midsummer. They include Chinese cabbage, leaf radish, mibuna, mizuna, mustards, pak choi and shungiku. Their great advantage is speed: many can be cut as baby leaves within a month, while late-summer sowings often suffer less flea beetle damage and provide useful autumn crops. They are tender and flavoursome rather than long-storing staples, but they are excellent for filling the salad gap from late summer into autumn, and under cover some leafy types can continue as winter salad leaves.

Parsnips are slow, deep-rooting biennials grown for their long white tap roots, which are at their sweetest after cold weather has turned starches into sugars. They take up the ground for a long season and the seedlings are small and slow to appear, but once established they need little more than clean soil, moisture while young and occasional weeding. Fresh seed improves germination; cold or dry soil and excessive sowing depth can also cause a blank row. The best roots come from deep, humus-rich, stone-free soil, preferably undug or improved for a previous crop rather than freshly manured.

Peas are one of the great rewards of early summer: a freshly picked pod, eaten straight from the plant, has a sweetness which disappears quickly after picking as the sugars turn to starch. They have long been a staple crop for canning, freezing and drying, but home-grown peas are at their best picked young and cooked or eaten almost immediately.

Potatoes can feed a household from a small plot, with dense foliage useful on newly prepared ground; check former grassland for wireworms first. They are grown from seed potatoes rather than true seed; the planted tuber produces leafy haulm above ground and new tubers below and near the soil surface. Those tubers must be kept covered, because light turns them green and poisonous. First earlies crop quickly and are useful for fresh new potatoes; second earlies follow; maincrops give higher yields and better winter storage but need more space and are more exposed to blight.

Radishes are among the fastest root crops and deserve a place for their speed alone: spring sowings can give mild, juicy roots when few other outdoor crops are ready. They are useful in odd corners, window boxes, under protection, or as a quick crop between slower vegetables. The familiar small red and red-white radishes are best eaten young, before heat, age or drought makes them hot, woody, hollow or soft. Winter radishes are a more substantial crop: they include white, pink, black and red-white types, grow for much longer, and can be grated, pickled, braised, stir-fried or stored in cool damp conditions after lifting in autumn.

Rhubarb is grown like a long-lived perennial vegetable, although it is usually cooked and eaten as a fruit. It produces tart spring stems, coloured green to red according to variety from large crowns, and the leaves are not eaten. Rhubarb suits cool climates and benefits from winter dormancy. Green-stemmed varieties are edible too: stem colour is not a ripeness test. Once established in a moist, well-drained, compost-rich corner, a crown can crop for many years with little attention beyond feeding, mulching, watering in dry springs and removing flower stems.

Salsify and scorzonera are closely related, old-fashioned root vegetables usually treated together. They are delicacies rather than staples: the roots are long, thin, tender and rather awkward to lift and clean, so usable yields can be modest. Salsify has creamy-coloured roots and is often called vegetable oyster because of its delicate, oyster-like flavour; scorzonera is similar but black-skinned. Both prefer deep, friable soil and direct sowing, and both can stand most winter weather.

Spinach is a quick leafy crop which can be available for much of the year with careful planning, but it needs steady moisture and rich soil to avoid bolting. There are summer and winter forms of true spinach, while New Zealand spinach is a separate, frost-tender plant often grown as a summer substitute in hot weather. Perpetual spinach, or spinach beet, is a type of leaf beet rather than true spinach. Choose the appropriate type for the season and pick tender leaves regularly.

Swedes are hardy brassica roots, closely related to turnips but slower growing, sweeter, more substantial and much more frost-resistant. Their flesh is usually orange or yellow, and the leaves arise from a neck above the root rather than directly from the root as in turnips. They are valuable winter vegetables because frost improves their flavour: after cold weather they become sweeter and are good boiled, mashed and seasoned. Swedes need a longer season than turnips, usually about a month more, but they are reliable as a late-sown second crop after early lettuce, carrots, broad beans or other early harvests if given enough room to swell.

Sweet corn is a warm-season crop grown for fresh cobs. Choose an early variety suited to local summers and a sunny, sheltered site. Full-sized cobs need good wind pollination, so plant a block of short rows.

Tomato plants are found in the majority of greenhouses during summer, producing a succession of fruit from early summer into autumn. They need constant care: water growing bags or pots regularly in summer and watch for pests and diseases. Home growers can choose flavours and varieties that are rarely sold commercially. Tall or cordon plants are trained with one central stem and their side-shoots removed throughout the season. They need warmth, light, steady root moisture, good ventilation and balanced fertility more than sheer feeding.

Outdoor tomatoes have plenty of flavour to offer, but need a warm, sunny, sheltered site and a variety suited to British summers. Choose plants labelled for outdoor cultivation; in cooler areas, cloches or other protection can make a crop more reliable. Tall cordon tomatoes need staking, side-shooting and stopping near the end of the season so existing fruit can ripen. Bush or determinate tomatoes need less pruning and can be grown under cloches or in containers. Keep low fruit clear of the ground where practical and check for slugs and blight.

Turnips are quick-growing brassica roots, faster and less hardy than swedes. They can be a mild, juicy spring crop if pulled young, a useful catch crop after summer harvests, or a small stored autumn root for winter stews. The roots are generally white-fleshed, with leaves growing directly from the root rather than from a raised neck. Early turnips can come to harvest in 60-80 days, sometimes almost as fast as radishes, while larger autumn roots need longer but should still be eaten before the hardest winter weather. Some varieties also provide useful edible leaves or turnip tops.
